title: Taurine Alleviates Sepsis-Induced Myocardial Injury by Inhibiting NF-κB Pathway-Mediated Inflammation, Mitochondrial Dysfunction, and Apoptosis

sections.abstract:
Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy (SICM) is a life-threatening complication characterized by cardiac dysfunction, inflammation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial impairment, with limited therapeutic options. Taurine, a naturally occurring amino acid with known anti-inflammatory and mitochondrial-stabilizing properties, may offer therapeutic benefits. However, its role in SICM is not well defined. This study aimed to evaluate the protective effects of taurine against SICM and elucidate its underlying mechanisms. A murine model of SICM was established via cecal ligation and puncture (CLP), and AC16 cardiomyocytes were stimulated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to mimic septic injury in vitro. Cardiac function was assessed by echocardiography; inflammatory cytokines and cardiac injury markers were measured via ELISA. Mitochondrial integrity and function were evaluated using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), oxygen consumption rate (OCR), and mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP). Apoptosis was analyzed by TUNEL staining, flow cytometry, and Western blot. Rescue experiments using an NF-κB activator were conducted to validate pathway involvement. The results showed that taurine treatment significantly improved cardiac function and survival rates in SICM mice, attenuated myocardial inflammation and oxidative stress, restored mitochondrial structure and function, and suppressed apoptosis. These beneficial effects were reversed upon NF-κB activation, indicating that taurine exerts its cardioprotective role primarily through inhibition of the NF-κB signaling pathway. In conclusion, this study provides the first evidence that taurine protects against SICM by alleviating NF-κB-driven inflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptosis, suggesting its potential as a therapeutic agent for sepsis-induced cardiac injury.

sections.introduction:
Sepsis is the life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, among which the heart is one of the most frequently affected organs [ 1 ]. It is the leading cause of death in hospitalized patients [ 2 ]. Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy (SICM) denotes any type of myocardial dysfunction caused by sepsis itself [ 3 ], which can increase sepsis mortality by approximately 50–70%, representing a critical global medical challenge [ 4 , 5 ]. SICM is characterized by the following key features: (1) reduced ventricular contractility, (2) left ventricular dilatation with normal or low filling pressures, and (3) right ventricular dysfunction and/or left ventricular dysfunction with diminished responsiveness to fluid therapy [ 6 ]. Diagnosis of SICM currently relies primarily on echocardiography combined with cardiac biomarkers such as brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) and troponin-T/I (TnT and TnI) [ 7 ]. Echocardiography serves as the gold standard for diagnosing SICM [ 8 ]. The current pathogenesis of SICM primarily involves excessive inflammatory response, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, cardiomyocyte apoptosis, microvascular dysfunction, and calcium dysregulation [ 9 – 11 ]. However, current clinical treatments for SICM are limited, primarily focusing on supportive care, underscoring an urgent need to explore novel and effective therapeutic strategies [ 9 ].

Following sepsis, various pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and endogenous damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) interact with myocardial Toll-like receptors (TLRs), activating the transcription nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) signaling pathway, which in turn induces the production of multiple proinflammatory cytokines, directly inhibiting myocardial contractility [ 10 , 11 ]. Moreover, excessive inflammatory mediators stimulate cells to produce large amounts of reactive oxygen species (ROS) [ 12 ], which damage myocardial mitochondrial membranes and trigger the opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP) [ 13 ]. This leads to a decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), mitochondrial swelling and damage, reduced mitochondrial respiratory capacity, and decreased ATP production [ 14 ]. Consequently, the energy required to maintain cardiac contractile function is significantly reduced, resulting in myocardial dysfunction [ 15 ]. Furthermore, upon MPTP opening, mitochondria release substantial amounts of DAMPs, including mtROS, mtDNA fragments, ATP, and cytochrome C, which further activate the NF-κB pathway and inflammatory response, forming a vicious cycle [ 16 ]. Ultimately, these lead to the activation of the apoptotic pathway and cell apoptosis [ 17 ]. Therefore, inhibiting inflammation and mitochondrial dysfunction is a key approach and strategy for treating SICM.

Taurine is a naturally occurring sulfur-containing amino acid and one of the most abundant amino acids found in eukaryotic organisms [ 18 ]. It is present in various animal tissues, with high concentrations in the myocardium, skeletal muscle, and brain [ 19 ]. Taurine plays crucial biological roles in inflammation, cellular redox, osmoregulation, energy metabolism, membrane structure stabilization, and modulation of calcium signaling [ 20 ]. Taurine accounts for approximately 50% of the total free amino acids in the heart and has been demonstrated to exert protective effects in various cardiac diseases [ 19 ]. In both human and animal models, cardiac taurine deficiency has been found to cause myocardial energy depletion and damage [ 21 ]. Conversely, taurine supplementation improves cardiac function and provides cardioprotective effects through mechanisms such as enhancing myocardial contractility, inhibiting myocardial cell apoptosis, regulating cardiac mitochondrial function, and suppressing cardiac inflammation and oxidative stress [ 19 , 22 , 23 ].

Taurine has been demonstrated to play a crucial role in sepsis. Clinical studies [ 24 , 25 ] have shown that taurine concentration decreases during sepsis, with a significant reduction as sepsis severity worsens or patient prognosis deteriorates, and its serum concentration is negatively correlated with disease severity. Additionally, the protective effects of taurine have also been further validated in animal models. Studies indicate that it significantly mitigates multiple organ injuries induced by sepsis, specifically encompassing the liver [ 26 ], lungs [ 27 , 28 ], kidneys [ 29 ], and diaphragm [ 30 ]. Although the aforementioned studies highlight taurine’s role and potential in sepsis-induced organ damage, none have specifically examined the heart as a core organ. Consequently, no research currently confirms taurine’s definitive effect on sepsis-induced myocardial injury. Specifically: First, although the heart is rich in taurine and its benefits in other cardiac pathologies have been demonstrated, there is a lack of direct evidence indicating whether taurine supplementation can directly improve sepsis-induced cardiac dysfunction (such as impaired contractile function). Second, it remains unclear whether taurine can mitigate hallmark pathological features of SICM-associated myocardial injury, such as excessive cytokine production, oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage, and cardiomyocyte apoptosis. Furthermore, if protective effects exist, the key molecular signaling pathways through which taurine exerts these potential cardioprotective actions remain undefined. Whether its myocardial protective effect is achieved by inhibiting the NF-κB pathway—the core pathway driving myocardial inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptosis in SICM—remains to be further investigated.

Therefore, this study aims to validate through in vivo and in vitro experiments whether taurine can improve SICM myocardial dysfunction and related pathological features by inhibiting the NF-κB pathway. The objective is to clarify its cardioprotective effects and mechanisms, thereby providing new therapeutic strategies.
sections.methods:
8–10 weeks male C57BL/6J mice (22–25 g) were purchased and housed at the Experimental Animal Center of the Air Force Medical University (Xi’an, China). Mice were maintained under controlled temperature (20–21℃) on a 12-hour light/dark cycle with ad libitum access to food and water. All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of the Air Force Medical University (Ethical Approval No. IACUC20210462) and strictly conducted in accordance with international guidelines for the ethical use of animals.

Following previous studies [ 31 ], a mouse model of sepsis was established by cecal puncture and ligation (CLP). Mice were randomly assigned to four groups: Sham group, Taurine group, CLP group, and CLP + Taurine group. Briefly, mice were anesthetized with 4–5% isoflurane. A 1-cm midline abdominal incision was made to expose the cecum. The cecum was ligated 1 cm from the distal end with 4 − 0 silk suture and punctured through once with a 20-gauge needle. The cecum was gently squeezed to extrude a small amount of fecal content, returned to the peritoneal cavity, and the abdomen was closed with continuous sutures. Sham-operated mice underwent identical procedures excluding ligation and puncture. All mice received subcutaneous injection of 0.5 ml sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for fluid resuscitation immediately after surgery. The taurine (200 mg/kg, T8691, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) dosage was selected based on previous studies [ 26 , 29 , 32 ]. Mice in the Taurine and CLP + Taurine groups received an intraperitoneal injection (i.p.) of taurine (200 mg/kg) dissolved in PBS 2 h post-surgery. Mice in the Sham and CLP groups received an equal volume of PBS vehicle via intraperitoneal injection. At 24 h post-surgery, echocardiography was performed, followed by euthanasia and collection of heart and blood samples for subsequent analyses.

The survival study protocol followed established methods [ 33 ]. Briefly, after sham or CLP surgery, survival was assessed every 4 h by three trained, blinded investigators until 72 h post-surgery. Survival curves were plotted using the Kaplan-Meier method, with intergroup differences compared using the log-rank test. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. The murine sepsis score (MSS) was assessed as previously described [ 34 ] and recorded by the same investigators at 12 h post-surgery. This scoring system quantifies seven indicators in mice: spontaneous activity, response to touch and auditory stimuli, posture, respiration rate and quality (labored breathing or gasping), and appearance (i.e., degree of piloerection). Each indicator is assigned a score ranging from 0 to 4, with a higher total score indicating more severe sepsis.

Mice were anesthetized with 2% isoflurane, chest hair was removed with depilatory cream, and mice were placed prone on a heated platform (37 °C). Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), left ventricular fractional shortening (LVFS), and cardiac output (CO) were measured using M-mode echocardiography in the parasternal long-axis view with a Vevo 3100 system (FujiFilm VisualSonics, Toronto, Canada) equipped with a high-frequency transducer. All measurements were averaged over three consecutive cardiac cycles. Echocardiographic images were acquired and analyzed by experienced technicians from the Analysis & Testing Laboratory for Life Sciences and Medicine of the Air Force Medical University, who were blinded to the treatment groups.

Apoptosis in heart tissue was assessed using the One-step TUNEL In Situ Apoptosis Kit (Green, FITC) (Elabscience, Wuhan, China) strictly following the manufacturer’s protocol. The ratio of TUNEL + nucleus was the proportion of TUNEL positive cells in the total number of cells. TUNEL-positive cells were quantified using ImageJ software. Specifically, at least three non-overlapping fields of view were randomly selected from each mouse heart section. The number of TUNEL-positive nuclei and the total number of DAPI-stained nuclei were counted in each field of view. The TUNEL-positive cell rate was ultimately calculated as the percentage of TUNEL-positive nuclei relative to the total number of nuclei in each field of view. The observation and counting are double-blinded.

The AC16 Human Cardiomyocyte cells (Servicebio, Wuhan, China) were cultured in high-glucose Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2. When cell confluency reaches 80–90%, proceed with the experiment and use the cells as recommended until the tenth passage [ 35 ]. Using a well-established experimental protocol previously reported [ 36 – 38 ], AC16 cells were treated with lipopolysaccharide (Catalog #2630, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) at a concentration of 10 µg/ml for 24 h to establish an in vitro sepsis injury model. To investigate taurine’s effects, AC16 cells were co-treated with LPS (10 µg/ml) and different concentrations of taurine (0, 10, 20, 40, 80 mM; Aladdin, Shanghai, China) for 24 h prior to assays. To investigate the function of NF-κB in AC16 cells, cells were treated with 1 µM NF-κB activator 1 (HY-134476, MCE, New Jersey, USA) for 1 h before LPS stimulation.

AC16 cell viability was assessed using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay (Life-iLab, Shanghai, China). Cells were seeded in 96-well plates. After 24 h, they were treated with LPS (10 µg/ml) and various concentrations of taurine (0, 10, 20, 40, 80 mM) for another 24 h. Control cells received no treatment. CCK-8 reagent was added to each well and incubated for 1.5 h. Absorbance (OD) was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader.

AC16 cells were seeded into 12-well plates and treated according to different groups. Apoptosis in AC16 cells was quantified using an Annexin V-FITC/PI Apoptosis Detection Kit (Simu Biotech, Tianjin, China) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Analysis was performed using a flow cytometer.

Mice blood was collected, centrifuged, and the supernatant was collected. Serum levels of interleukin-1β(IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), pro-brain natriuretic peptide (pro-BNP), and cardiac troponin-I (cTn-I) were measured using ELISA kits according to the respective manufacturer’s protocols. The ELISA kits for IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α were procured from Boster (Wuhan, China), while the kits for pro-BNP and cTn-I were obtained from Elabscience (Wuhan, China).

Mice were euthanized 24 h post-CLP. Hearts were perfused with cold saline, fixed in 10% paraformaldehyde for 48 h, embedded in paraffin, sectioned (5 μm thickness), and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Images were captured using a digital microscope and analyzed with ImageJ software.

Small pieces of myocardial tissue were fixed overnight in 2.5% glutaraldehyde at 4 °C, post-fixed in 1% osmium tetroxide, dehydrated through a graded ethanol series, and embedded in epoxy resin. Ultrathin Sect. (70 nm) were cut, stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate, and examined under a TEM to assess mitochondrial ultrastructure. Perform a semi-quantitative analysis of myocardial mitochondria using the previously described Flameng mitochondrial scoring system [ 39 ]. Three specimens per group were randomly selected, with five fields of view photographed at equal magnification per specimen. Approximately 20 mitochondria were randomly selected for analysis within each field of view. Each mitochondrion was scored according to the aforementioned criteria, and the average score per field of view was calculated. A higher average score indicates more severe mitochondrial damage. The Flameng scoring criteria are as follows: Score 0: Normal structure with well-preserved mitochondrial granules. Score 1: Normal structure but granules absent. Score 2: Swollen mitochondria with clarification of the matrix. Score 3: Disruption of mitochondrial crests with clarification as well as condensation of the matrix. Score 4: Disruption of the crests and loss of integrity of the mitochondrial inner and outer membranes.

Total RNA was extracted from heart tissue using TRIzol reagent. cDNA was synthesized using a reverse transcription kit. RT-qPCR was performed using SYBR Green premix on a CFX96 Real-Time PCR System. Gene expression levels were normalized to GAPDH and calculated using the 2^-ΔΔCt method. Primer sequences are listed in S1.

The total protein was extracted in Cell lysis buffer containing protease inhibitors for western blot. Proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. Membranes were blocked with rapid blocking buffer and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, followed by appropriate secondary antibodies. At the end of the incubation with the primary and secondary antibodies, the PVDF membrane was washed three times with TBST, for 10 min each time. Protein bands were visualized using chemiluminescent HRP substrate and imaged. Densitometric analysis was performed using ImageJ software. Primary antibodies used were: anti-NRF2 (1:1000, GB113808 , Servicebio, China), anti-Bcl-2 (1:1000, bsm-61074R, Bioss, China), anti-Bax (1:5000, ER0907, HUABIO, China), anti-Caspase-3/Cleaved Caspase-3 (1:1000, WL02117, Wanleibio, China), anti-IκBα (1:1000, #15595, Cell Signaling Technology, USA), anti-p-IκBα (Ser32) (1:1000, #2859, Cell Signaling Technology, USA), anti-p-NF-κB p65 (Ser536) (1:1000, #3033, Cell Signaling Technology, USA), anti-NF-κB p65 (1:1000, #8242, Cell Signaling Technology, USA), anti-β-Actin (1:20000, 66009-1-IG, Proteintech, China), anti-Rabbit IgG (1:5000,S0001, Affinity, China), and anti-Mouse IgG (1:5000, S0002, Affinity, China).

Myocardial tissue was homogenized in PBS (1:9, g: mL). Homogenates were centrifuged at 10,000 g for 10–15 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was collected. Levels of superoxide dismutase (SOD), malondialdehyde (MDA), and glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px) were measured using specific assay kits (Servicebio, Wuhan, China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. OD values were recorded using a microplate reader and corresponding concentrations were calculated.

AC16 cells were seeded into 12-well plates and treated according to different groups. Intracellular ROS levels were assessed using a ROS Detection Kit (Servicebio, Wuhan, China). Cells were incubated with 500 µL/well of DCFH-DA working solution for 30 min at 37 °C in the dark. The solution was removed, cells were washed three times with PBS, fluorescence images were captured using a fluorescence microscope, and fluorescence intensity was quantified using ImageJ software.

OCR detection was performed according to the previously reported mature solution [ 40 ]. Specifically, mitochondrial respiratory function in AC16 cells was assessed using the Seahorse XF analyser (Agilent, USA) according to the manufacturer’s mitochondrial stress test protocol. Cells were first seeded at a density of 10,000 cells per well in XF cell culture microplates (Agilent, USA), then treated according to different groups. Specifically: the Control group and Taurine group were treated with PBS solution and 40 mM taurine respectively for 24 h; the LPS group was treated with LPS (10 µg/ml) for 24 h; and the LPS + Taurine group was treated with both LPS (10 µg/ml) and taurine (40 mM) for 24 h. The medium was then replaced with Seahorse XF DMEM medium (pH 7.4) containing 1 mM sodium pyruvate, 2 mM glutamine, and 10 mM glucose. After equilibration for one hour in a 37 °C CO₂-free incubator, measurements were taken. Following baseline readings, sequential injections of oligomycin (1.5 µM), FCCP (1.0 µM), and a mixture of rotenone/antimycin A (0.5 µM each) were administered to measure and obtain real-time cellular metabolic function. All reagents were sourced from the XF Cell Mitochondrial Stress Test Kit (Agilent, USA). Following each assay, viable cells were counted via Hoechst 33,342 staining, with data normalised to equal cell numbers. Results were expressed as pmol/min/10,000 cells. Data points for each experimental condition were collected from at least three replicates, with each assay performed in triplicate.

Alterations in mitochondrial membrane potential were examined using a Mitochondrial Membrane Potential Assay Kit (with JC-1) (Elabscience, Wuhan, China). AC16 cells were seeded into 12-well plates and treated according to different groups. JC-1 working fluid was prepared according to the instructions. The JC-1 working solution was employed to incubate cells for 1 h at 37 °C in the dark, followed by three washes with PBS on a shaker, each with a duration of 5 min. Finally cells were imaged using fluorescent Microscopy. Fluorescence intensity was quantified using ImageJ software.

AC16 cells were seeded onto slides and processed according to different groupings. Fix cells with 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 20 min, then permeabilize in 0.3% Triton X-100 solution at room temperature for 15 min. Block cells with 5% BSA for 30 min. After blocking, cells were incubated overnight at 4 °C with anti-NF-κB p65 (1:400,#8242, Cell Signaling Technology, USA), followed by incubation at room temperature for 2 h with the appropriate secondary antibody. Cell nuclei were stained with DAPI. Cells were washed three times with PBS for 5 min each step. Images were acquired using a confocal microscope.

Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0. Differences between two groups were analyzed using the unpaired Student’s t-test. Differences among multiple groups were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. Survival data were analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method with the log-rank test. A p-value less than 0.05 ( p < 0.05) was considered statistically significant. Graphical abstract was created with BioGDP. com [ 41 ].
sections.results:
The cecal puncture and ligation (CLP) model is the most widely used in vivo model for polymicrobial sepsis and mimics intra-abdominal infections [ 42 ], thus we established a mouse model of CLP-induced sepsis to investigate the effect of taurine on SICM. Mice received intraperitoneal injection of taurine (200 mg/kg) 2 h after Sham or CLP surgery (Fig. 1 A). To assess the impact of taurine on the survival rate of SICM mice, we conducted a 72-hour survival observation and performed survival analysis using the Kaplan-Meier method. Results demonstrated that taurine treatment significantly improved mouse survival rates: the 72-hour survival rate in the CLP group was 30%, whereas the CLP + Taurine group showed an increase to 50% (Log-rank test, p < 0.05). Further analysis of survival curve morphology revealed a plateau phase near the 50% survival rate in both groups. Following standard methodology for handling such plateaus [ 43 ], median survival time was calculated from the midpoint of the plateau. As shown in Figure B (where the dashed line marks the median survival point), the median survival time in the CLP group was 40 h, whereas in the CLP + Taurine group it was significantly prolonged to 65 h. These findings suggest that taurine therapy not only enhances short-term survival rates but also significantly delays the progression of mortality, thereby securing a critical time window for myocardial injury repair and subsequent clinical interventions. Furthermore, murine sepsis score (MSS) was significantly reduced in taurine-treated CLP mice compared to the CLP group (Fig. 1 C). These findings demonstrate that taurine significantly improves survival and clinical outcomes in CLP-induced SICM mice.

SICM is characterized by myocardial dysfunction such as reduced myocardial contractility [ 44 ]. Fractional shortening, ejection fraction, and cardiac output play a crucial role in predicting cardiac function [ 45 ]. Therefore, cardiac function in mice was examined by echocardiography at 24 h after CLP. The results showed that compared to the Sham group, CLP mice exhibited significantly decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), left ventricular fractional shortening (LVFS), and cardiac output (CO), indicating impaired contractility. In contrast, taurine treatment significantly restored LVEF, LVFS, and CO in CLP mice, suggesting improved myocardial contractility and cardiac function (Fig. 1 D-G). Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of myocardial tissue showed normal cardiomyocyte structure in Sham mice, whereas CLP mice exhibited myocardial edema, disorganized fibers, and inflammatory infiltration. Similarly, taurine treatment markedly attenuated pathological alterations in myocardial tissues compared to SICM model group (Fig. 1 H). Additionally, Serum levels of myocardial injury biomarkers, cardiac troponin-I (cTn-I) and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), were significantly increased in CLP mice. However, taurine treatment markedly reduced serum cTn-I and BNP levels in these mice (Fig. 1 I-J). These results confirm the successful establishment of the SICM model and demonstrate that taurine effectively improves myocardial contractility, cardiac function, and reduces myocardial injury in SICM mice.

Inflammatory cytokines play a crucial role in the progression of inflammatory cardiomyopathies [ 46 ]. Cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) have been identified as myocardial suppressors that directly impair the contractility of SICM myocardium [ 3 , 9 ]. Therefore, we evaluated the levels of inflammatory factors in mice. The results showed that CLP significantly elevated serum levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α, whereas taurine treatment markedly reduced these cytokines (Fig. 2 A-C). In addition, taurine treatment also significantly reduced the mRNA expression of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α in the myocardial tissues of SICM mice. (Fig. 2 D–F). These results indicate that taurine effectively reduces myocardial depressant factor levels and attenuates systemic and cardiac inflammation in SICM.

Inhibiting oxidative stress protects cardiac mitochondria, reduces inflammation, and improves cardiac function [ 47 ]. To evaluate oxidative stress, we therefore measured levels of malondialdehyde (MDA), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px) in myocardial tissue, which reflect the oxidative stress activity in the cells [ 48 ]. Compared with the Sham group, CLP-induced mice exhibited increased MDA levels and decreased SOD and GSH-Px activity, indicating oxidative stress. On the contrary, taurine supplementation significantly reduced MDA levels and restored SOD and GSH-Px activity (Fig. 2 G-I). Additionally, we examined the protein expression levels of Nuclear Factor Erythroid-Derived 2-Like 2 (Nrf2), a transcription factor primarily involved in oxidative stress responses. Western blot analysis revealed that CLP surgery significantly reduced Nrf2 protein expression in myocardium compared with the Sham group, while taurine treatment markedly reversed this decrease (Fig. 2 J-K). These findings suggest that taurine holds potential value in alleviating oxidative stress associated with SICM.

We next used the AC16 Human Cardiomyocyte cells (AC16 cells) to investigate the role of taurine in sepsis induced by LPS treatment. To determine the optimal therapeutic concentration of taurine for AC16 cells, cells were treated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (10 µg/ml) and various concentrations of taurine (0, 10, 20, 40, 80 mM) for 24 h, and viability was assessed using CCK-8. Taurine concentrations up to 40 mM significantly enhanced the viability of LPS-treated AC16 cells (Fig. 2 L). Therefore, this concentration was selected as the optimal concentration for the subsequent experiments since 80 mM taurine slightly decreased cell survival (Fig. 2 L), suggesting potential cytotoxicity at this dose. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were assessed using fluorescent probes, showing that LPS (10 µg/mL) significantly increased intracellular ROS fluorescence intensity and levels compared to the control. Taurine supplementation (40 mM) markedly reduced ROS generation (Fig. 2 M-N). These findings collectively demonstrate that taurine supplementation mitigates inflammation and oxidative stress damage in SICM.

Mitochondrial damage is a key mechanism underlying sepsis-induced myocardial dysfunction [ 17 ]. Therefore, we used transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to evaluate mitochondrial morphology in mouse hearts and quantified mitochondrial damage using the Flameng semi-quantitative mitochondrial scoring system. TEM results showed (Fig. 3 A-B) that the cardiac mitochondrial structure in the Sham group was normal, whereas the CLP-induced sepsis model caused severe mitochondrial ultrastructural damage, manifested as reduced mitochondrial number, marked swelling, disrupted cristae architecture, decreased density, and significantly elevated Flameng scores. Taurine treatment significantly alleviated these damages compared to the CLP group, with a marked decrease in Flameng scores, indicating preserved mitochondrial structure (Fig. 3 A-B).

Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) is a key biomarker reflecting mitochondrial function, cellular metabolism, and respiratory capacity [ 49 ]. To explore the effect of taurine on mitochondrial function, we further measured the OCR of AC16 cells using a seahorse cell energy metabolism analyzer to evaluate key parameters of mitochondrial respiratory function, including basal respiration, maximal respiration and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production. The normalized OCR results (Fig. 3 C-F) show that, compared with those of control cells, the basal respiration, maximum respiration and ATP production of AC16 cells treated with LPS (10 µg/ml) were significantly reduced. However, treatment with taurine (40 mM) significantly reversed the reduction in mitochondrial respiratory function parameters caused by LPS (Fig. 3 C-F), indicating that taurine improved the mitochondrial respiratory dysfunction caused by LPS. Mitochondrial membrane potential is one of the important indicators for evaluating the normal function of mitochondria [ 50 ]. It not only reflects the integrity of mitochondrial function, but also has significant impacts on ATP synthesis, ion transport, regulation of apoptosis, and antioxidant activities [ 50 ]. We thus evaluated the mitochondrial function by measuring the mitochondrial membrane potential using JC-1 dye. The results showed that cells treated with LPS exhibited an increased green fluorescence of JC-1 monomers, indicating mitochondrial dysfunction. However, treatment with taurine inhibited the increase in mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) induced by LPS (Fig. 3 G-H). These findings collectively indicate that mitochondrial dysfunction occurs in AC16 cardiac muscle cells after LPS treatment. Supplementing taurine can effectively alleviate and reverse the aforementioned mitochondrial damage and dysfunction.

Apoptosis plays a crucial role in SICM pathogenesis, and inflammation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial damage can induce and exacerbate it [ 51 ]. We thus assessed apoptosis using TUNEL staining, flow cytometry, and Western blotting. TUNEL staining revealed a significant increase in TUNEL-positive (TUNEL + green) cells in the CLP group compared to Sham group. Taurine treatment greatly reduced the number of TUNEL + cells in septic heart tissues (Fig. 4 A-B). Similarly, the findings of Flow Cytometry with Annexin Staining showed that LPS treatment (10 µg/ml, 24 h) significantly increased the apoptosis rate in AC16 cells, while taurine (40 mM) treatment markedly alleviated LPS-induced apoptosis (Fig. 4 C-D). Western blot analysis further corroborated these findings, showing that CLP significantly increased myocardial levels of pro-apoptotic proteins Bax and Cleaved-Caspase-3 while decreasing the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2. Taurine treatment reversed these protein expression changes (Fig. 4 E-H). Collectively, these results demonstrate that taurine plays a significant role in inhibiting sepsis-induced cardiomyocyte apoptotic pathways.

Nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) plays a central role in cardiac inflammation and damage during septic cardiac dysfunction [ 52 ]. Therefore, we evaluated the NF-κB signaling pathway. In vitro immunofluorescence staining showed increased nuclear translocation of NF-κB p65 in AC16 cells after LPS treatment (10 µg/ml, 24 h). Taurine treatment reduced this LPS-induced nuclear translocation (Fig. 5 A). Similarly, western blot analysis of mice showed that CLP surgery significantly increased the phosphorylation levels of p65 and IKBα while reducing the expression levels of total IKBα protein compared to the control group. Notably, taurine partially reversed these CLP-induced changes, as evidenced by decreased phosphorylation levels of p65 and IKBα, as well as restored IKBα expression levels (Fig. 5 B-C). These findings indicate that taurine inhibits sepsis-activated NF-κB signaling pathway both in vivo and in vitro. Collectively, the results indicate that taurine may exert a protective role in SICM by inhibiting the activation of the NF-κB signaling pathway.

To further investigate whether the protective effect of taurine is primarily mediated through the NF-κB pathway, we conducted rescue experiments using a specific NF-κB agonist (NF-κB activator 1) to pretreat AC16 cells prior to LPS stimulation. Treatment with the NF-κB agonist significantly attenuated the protective effects of taurine in LPS-treated AC16 cells. Specifically, ROS fluorescence results showed that the addition of NF-κB activator 1 significantly weakened the inhibitory effect of taurine on ROS production, as evidenced by a significant increase in cellular ROS fluorescence intensity and levels in the LPS + Taurine + NF-κB activator 1 group compared to the LPS + Taurine group (Fig. 6 A-B). Additionally, mitochondrial membrane potential detection results showed that, compared to the LPS + Taurine group, the mitochondrial membrane potential level in the LPS + Taurine + NF-κB activator 1 group significantly decreased, indicating that NF-κB activator treatment significantly reversed the protective effect of taurine against LPS-induced mitochondrial dysfunction (Fig. 6 C-D). Flow cytometry analysis showed that NF-κB activator treatment reversed the anti-apoptotic effect of taurine, as evidenced by a significant increase in apoptosis rate in the LPS + NF-κB activator 1 group compared to the LPS + Taurine group (Fig. 6 E-F). Similarly, Western blot analysis also indicated that activation of the NF-κB pathway weakened the inhibitory effect of taurine on apoptosis, leading to reduced Bcl-2 protein expression and increased levels of Bax protein and cleaved-Caspase3 protein (Fig. 6 G-J). These results collectively demonstrate that activation of the NF-κB pathway can significantly reverse the protective effect of taurine on LPS-stimulated AC16 cells. Collectively, these results strongly support the notion that taurine exerts its protective effects in SICM by inhibiting the NF-κB signaling pathway.

sections.discussion:
SICM is a severe complication associated with high mortality rates in sepsis. Due to its complex pathogenesis and limited treatment options, SICM remains a major clinical challenge requiring urgent solutions, highlighting the need for novel therapies [ 11 ]. Taurine, as an endogenous substance and nutritional supplement, has been demonstrated to exert a wide range of protective effects [ 18 , 19 , 22 ]. In this study, we demonstrated for the first time that taurine alleviates SICM by enhancing myocardial contractility, reducing inflammation and oxidative stress, preserving mitochondrial ultrastructure and function, and inhibiting cardiomyocyte apoptosis. These findings provide a novel perspective on taurine as a potential treatment for SICM.

Inflammation and oxidative stress are one of the main mechanisms leading to SICM, not only directly reducing myocardial contractility [ 11 , 47 , 53 ], but also causing myocardial energy metabolism collapse and cell death [ 54 ]. Inflammation can lead to oxidative stress, which in turn can further exacerbate inflammation. Substantial evidence indicates that inhibiting inflammation and oxidative stress exerts a clear protective effect on SICM [ 55 – 57 ]. The anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects of taurine have been validated in various diseases. It can reduce cardiac inflammation and oxidative stress in rats to alleviate myocardial ischemia injury [ 58 ], alleviate lipid peroxidation, oxidative stress, and pro-inflammatory factor release induced by malathion in rats [ 59 ], and can also alleviate oxidative stress in porcine mammary epithelial cells by Nrf2-MAPK signaling [ 60 ]. Therefore, we speculated that taurine might protect SICM through the above mechanisms. Excitingly, the findings align with our expectations: taurine effectively protects cardiac function, reduces inflammatory responses, and lowers the protein levels of the transcription factor Nrf2 and multiple oxidative stress markers, thereby shielding the heart from SICM damage. Nrf2 is a transcription factor for multiple antioxidant genes and has been demonstrated to reduce oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis in various diseases, thereby exerting significant protective effects [ 61 – 63 ]. Although the NF-κB p65 subunit can directly inhibit the Nrf2 pathway at the transcriptional level [ 64 ], this study also suggests the possibility that taurine may exert direct mitochondrial protective effects by regulating Nrf2 to alleviate inflammatory storms and oxidative stress. Further exploration and investigation are warranted. Moreover, immune cells are the core drivers of myocardial inflammatory processes, with macrophages serving as the primary immune population in the heart [ 65 ]. Their functional polarization plays a particularly critical role in the immunopathology of sepsis. Specifically, M1 macrophages dominate pro-inflammatory responses, exacerbating tissue damage, while M2 macrophages exert anti-inflammatory and reparative effects. The dynamic equilibrium between M1 and M2 subpopulations directly determines the trajectory of myocardial immune responses, and its disruption constitutes a major mechanism leading to excessive inflammation and cardiac injury [ 66 , 67 ]. At the same time, other immune cells also play a crucial role in the inflammatory cascade. Therefore, investigating the regulatory role of taurine in modulating macrophage polarization and other key immune cell subtypes during septic cardiomyopathy represents a highly valuable research direction for elucidating its cardioprotective mechanisms.

Mitochondrial dysfunction plays a pivotal role in SICM [ 7 , 68 ]. Specifically, mitochondrial dysfunction mediates cardiac dysfunction in sepsis through multiple interrelated core mechanisms, forming cascading reactions and vicious cycles. Myocardial dysfunction primarily arises via the following mitochondrial injury pathways [ 11 , 12 , 69 – 71 ]: (1) Electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation abnormalities: Inflammatory mediators damage electron transport chain complexes, causing oxidative phosphorylation uncoupling and insufficient ATP production, leading to myocardial energy crisis, (2) Mitochondrial structural damage: Mitochondrial swelling, cristae disruption, and membrane rupture compromise ultrastructure and functional integrity; (3) Oxidative/nitric stress imbalance: Dysfunction triggers excessive ROS and reactive nitrogen species production, jointly attacking proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids; (4) Proton leakage and uncoupling: Abnormal proton channel opening exacerbates oxidative phosphorylation decoupling and energy dissipation; (5) Mitochondrial permeability transition: Triggering matrix leakage and membrane potential collapse, constituting a critical step in apoptosis initiation; (6) Calcium homeostasis disruption: Abnormal calcium uptake/release induces intracellular overload, impairing contractility while exacerbating oxidative damage and MPT activation; (7) Imbalance in quality control: Dysregulation of fission/fusion, impaired mitochondrial autophagy, and hindered biosynthesis lead to accumulation of abnormal mitochondria; (8) Mitochondrial DNA damage: Direct attacks on mtDNA by ROS and other factors affect respiratory chain proteins encoded by mtDNA, forming a vicious cycle of dysfunction. These mechanisms intertwine and synergise, disrupting cardiomyocyte function through multiple pathways—including impaired energy metabolism, structural damage, and abnormal signal activation—ultimately driving the progression of SICM. This study reveals that taurine mitigates mitochondrial ultrastructural damage in septic mice, reduces ROS levels, improves membrane potential and respiratory function, and inhibits apoptosis. These findings suggest taurine may exert protective effects by modulating several key pathways. This not only expands the understanding of taurine’s application in cardiac diseases but also offers a novel potential strategy for the prevention and treatment of SICM. Furthermore, taurine may exert direct protective effects by regulating other mitochondrial biological processes. Future research should focus on elucidating this complex mechanism to systematically clarify taurine’s mitochondrial protective mechanisms in SICM.

NF-κB is a core transcription factor mediating SICM inflammatory responses [ 51 , 52 ]. In sepsis, degradation of IκBα leads to nuclear translocation of NF-κB p65, driving proinflammatory factor expression and subsequently triggering mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis [ 16 , 72 ]. This study confirms that taurine effectively inhibits activation of the myocardial NF-κB pathway, and its protective effect can be reversed by NF-κB activators, indicating that this pathway is a key mechanism for taurine’s cardioprotective action. This finding aligns with the widely accepted research consensus that inhibiting the NF-κB pathway is a crucial strategy for mitigating tissue damage [ 73 , 74 ]., and the protective effects of taurine in various disease models are consistently associated with its suppression of NF-κB [ 75 – 78 ]. Although this study demonstrates that taurine’s protective effects are closely associated with the inhibition of NF-κB, a core inflammatory pathway, the development of septic cardiomyopathy involves complex signalling networks. Consequently, taurine may also exert its protective effects on SICM through other pathways such as MAPK and SRF. For instance, the MAPK pathway, a key stress response pathway, plays a significant role in influencing cardiac gene expression, contractility, extracellular matrix remodelling, and cardiac inflammatory responses [ 79 ]. Inhibition of this pathway has been demonstrated to alleviate SICM [ 80 ]. Taurine has also been demonstrated to exert protective effects against septic lung injury by inhibiting the p38/MAPK pathway [ 27 ]. Furthermore, serum response factor (SRF) signaling serves as a pivotal regulator of cytoskeletal and metabolic gene expression, playing a crucial role in modulating cardiac mitochondrial function [ 81 ]. Its dysregulation may lead to increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, loss of membrane potential, and reduced ATP generation [ 82 , 83 ], with these alterations being closely associated with the pathological processes of SICM. Consequently, future research should employ omics analyses to further investigate the signaling networks regulated by taurine in SICM.

Taurine, as an endogenous amino acid and nutritional supplement, is widely sourced, cost-effective, and has a long history of safe use in the food industry [ 84 – 86 ]. Clinical studies (e.g., intravenous administration of 5 g [ 87 ], continuous oral intake for 6 months [ 88 ] and 8 weeks [ 81 ] have reported no serious adverse reactions at corresponding doses, providing evidence for its application in critical care settings. However, it must be emphasized that the safety of any therapeutic agent, including taurine, is highly dependent on dosage and clinical context. While existing evidence is encouraging, the optimal safe dosage regimen must be carefully determined in the context of severe physiological disruption caused by sepsis to avoid potential adverse effects. Therefore, while taurine demonstrates significant potential as an adjunctive therapy for sepsis due to its favorable safety profile, future studies must further elucidate its pharmacokinetic characteristics in the SICM model and precisely define its optimal therapeutic window.

This study retains certain limitations that warrant further investigation. Firstly, the research employed only male animal models; subsequent studies should incorporate female animals to examine the influence of sex and sex hormones on the therapeutic response to taurine, thereby providing evidence for precision clinical treatment. Secondly, although taurine was found to exert its effects by inhibiting the NF-κB pathway, the specific upstream targets and distinctions from known inhibitors remain unclear. Further clarification of its specific mechanism of action is required. Thirdly, the taurine dosage employed was based on prior literature. Systematic dose-gradient experiments should be conducted in future, validated in more complex large animal models, to determine its pharmacokinetic characteristics and optimal therapeutic time window. Furthermore, this study assessed mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation but did not concurrently measure ECAR, a key glycolytic indicator. Subsequent research should integrate simultaneous OCR/ECAR monitoring with metabolomics analysis to comprehensively elucidate taurine’s regulatory role within the energy metabolism network during septic cardiomyopathy.
sections.conclusion: In summary, this study provides the first evidence that taurine exerts significant protective effects against SICM by inhibiting the NF-κB signaling pathway, thereby alleviating inflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage, and apoptosis. Future research should further elucidate and expand the intrinsic mechanisms by which taurine protects SICM and systematically evaluate its pharmacokinetics and long-term efficacy in large animal models. This will lay a critical foundation for its clinical translation and offer new breakthroughs and hope for the clinical diagnosis and treatment of septic cardiomyopathy.
